newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu tells Arafat condolences not enough.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu tells Arafat condolences not enough.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu rejected Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's telephoned condolences after the Jerusalem bombings on Wednesday and told him he must do more to fight terror, the prime minister's spokesman said.

Netanyahu's director of communications, David Bar-Illan, told Reuters it would be "virtually impossible" to negotiate peace with the Palestinian Authority unless it "changed its attitude to terrorism" and stepped up activity against it.
"Arafat called the prime minister and asked to express his condolences after the attack in Jerusalem," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said.

"The prime minister told him in a tough conversation, a very tough conversation, that he is not satisfied with an expression of sorrow and that he demands Arafat act resolutely against the terrorist organisations and their infrastructure," Bazak said.

Eighteen people were killed on Wednesday when two explosions tore through a crowded outdoor market in Jewish West Jerusalem. Police said the attack was apparently the work of Moslem militant suicide bombers.
Bar-Illan accused Arafat of having given a "green light to terrorist organisations" to attack Israelis, a charge the prime minister first levelled after a Tel Aviv cafe bombing in March.
"The world will have to realise and the Palestinian Authority will have to realise that it is either violence and terrorism or a peace process. They cannot have it both ways," Bar-Illan said.
Arafat's office said the Palestinian leader telephoned his condolences to Netanyahu and Israeli President Ezer Weizman and wished those injured a speedy recovery.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak also telephoned Netanyahu to voice his condolences and promised to speak to Arafat about the prime minister's demands to crack down on terrorism, Bazak said.

"The prime minister told Arafat that recently Israel repeatedly warned about the need for Palestinian Authority action against terror groups and cooperation in the war against terrorism, something that Arafat pledged to do," Bazak said.

"The exact opposite happened. The prime minister told Arafat that the Palestinian Authority encouraged the violence and incitement and did not arrest Hamas and Islamic Jihad activists nor battle the terrorist infrastructure.
"And what was worse, senior elements in the Palestinian police were involved in those attacks," Bazak added.

Israel recently arrested four Palestinian police officers who it said planned to attack Jewish settlers in the West Bank. It accused the chief of Palestinian police of involvement in the alleged plan.
Netanyahu won election last year on platform pledging to boost security for Israelis stunned by a wave of suicide bombings in 1996.

He has made a Palestinian Authority crackdown on Moslem militants a condition for resuming formal peace talks which broke down in March over the start of construction of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Arafat has said he was making a "100 percent effort" to stop Palestinian attacks in Israel but could not guarantee complete success.
Bazak said Netanyahu would convene his security cabinet later on Wednesday in the wake of the bombings.
